rationale: A wins because it understands the central tension: "positive adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow, still unprofitable on a net basis, still carrying significant debt." That is a reporter-shaped story, not a victory lap. B has usable bones, but it keeps smuggling in mythology, especially "Three Years After Its Pandemic Crash, Peloton Has More Loyal Subscribers Than Ever," which asks the founder to pitch facts the update did not give them.
gaps_in_A: "Peloton stopped selling bikes and started renting them" is overclaimed. The update says Peloton is expanding rentals nationwide, not abandoning sales.
"$2,000+ upfront purchase" and "The $2,000 bike" are invented price anchors. Useful color, except it is not in the supplied facts, so it cannot carry the angle.
"what Peloton now is" oversells a rental expansion into an identity rewrite. The business-model angle works, but that phrase outruns the proof.
The rental and consumer-affordability angles partly duplicate each other. They are different enough to keep, but only if one stays on unit economics and the other gets a real named customer story.
gaps_in_B: "Peloton's CEO Cut $200M" and "What Did He Actually Slash?" personalize the cuts beyond the facts. The update says cuts happened under a new CEO, not that he personally designed them.
"He" invents the CEO's gender. Tiny word, big credibility leak.
"Three Years After Its Pandemic Crash" and "prevailing frame since roughly 2022" import an external narrative that was not supplied. A contrarian angle needs receipts, not vibes in a blazer.
"What Keeps 6 Million Peloton Subscribers Paying" conflates members with paying subscribers. The update says total members exceed 6 million; it does not say all are paying subscribers.
